evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: Landulf II(" c". 825 – 879) was Bishop and Count of Capua.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: He was the youngest of four sons of Landulf I, gastald of Capua.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: As a young man, he entered the church.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: When his father died, his eldest brother, Lando, succeeded him.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: On the death of the bishop of Capua, Paulinus, Lando made Landulf bishop of the city.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: Lando died in 861 and his young son, Lando II was deposed only a few months later by Landulf's other elder brother, Pando.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: Pando too died soon thereafter( 862 or 863) and a succession crisis broke out.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: Pando's son Pandenulf was shoved aside and Landulf, though bishop, took the Capuan throne in 863.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: However, the other branches of the family refused to recognize the usurpation and began seizing much of the county for themselves, leaving Landulf II only in control of the town of Capua proper.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: Isolated, Landulf II invited Saracen mercenaries to ravage the lands of his familiars, a move which much alarmed his neighbors( including the pope).

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: In 866, the deposed Pandenulf appealed to Emperor Louis II, then visiting Monte Cassino, to act against his uncle.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: The Emperor promptly besieged Capua and divested Landulf II, but instead of restoring Pandenulf, decided to pass the county of Capua over to the marquis Lambert I of Spoleto.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: This arrangement did not last long.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: In 871, Lambert was involved in a rebellion against Louis II orchestrated by Adelchis of Benevento.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: In the aftermath, Louis II deposed Lambert and restored Landulf II as count of Capua.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: As a condition, Landulf II swore off deploying Saracens in the county.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: Upon the death of Louis( 875), who had strictly enforced peace amongst the Christians of the Mezzogiorno, Landulf II allied himself with the Saracens, but in 877, Pope John VIII convinced him to ally himself to the papacy against the Muslims.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: He spent the next years defending the Amalfi Coast with his navy in return for tribute.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: Landulf II died in 879, undisputed count of Capua, and a succession crisis broke out again between his nephews Lando II( son of Lando), Pandenulf( son of Pando) and Lando III( son of Landenulf of Teano).

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: In the chronicle of Erchempert, of whom he was a contemporary, Landulf II of Capua is the chief villain, portrayed as a dabbler in mysticism and black magic, Saracen ally and enemy of Christendom.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: Erchempert's portrayal of Landulf II was the inspiration for the character of evil duke and magician Klingsor in Wolfram von Eschenbach's medieval epic" Parzival".

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: Eschenbach's epic was later translated into the famous nineteenth- century opera" Parsifal" by Richard Wagner.

evidence.title: Landulf II of Capua
evidence.text: As American film director George Lucas is frequently said to have looked to" Parsifal" for inspiration in his creation of the" Star Wars" saga, Landulf II of Capua, via this long chain of association, is the closest historical source for the villainous Darth Vader.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: Jordan I  (after 1046 – 1091), count of Aversa and prince of Capua from 1078 to his death, was the eldest son and successor of Prince Richard I of Capua and Fressenda, a daughter of Tancred of Hauteville and his second wife, also named Fressenda, and the nephew of Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: He, according to William of Apulia, "equalled in his virtues both the duke and his father."

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: In 1071, Jordan briefly rebelled against his father with the support of his uncle, Ranulf.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: In 1078, while his father was besieging Naples with Robert Guiscard, Jordan and Robert, count of Loritello, were ravaging the Abruzzi, then papal territory.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: He, his father, and the duke were all excommunicated, when, suddenly, his father fell ill, retired to Capua, reconciled with the church, and died.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: Jordan, fearing to rule under the ban of the church, called off the siege of Naples and went to Rome to reconcile himself to Pope Gregory VII and rectify his relations with the church, of which his father had been both servant and protector.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: It appears that he intended to take up the position of his father "vis-a-vis" the papacy and to return to unfriendly relations with the duke of Apulia, for Gregory visited Capua a mere three months after Richard's death and Jordan, probably with papal prodding, began fomenting revolt in the Guiscard's lands.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: The revolt, the widely supported and well-organised, was ineffectual in really curbing Robert's influence and power.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: One of his chief advisors was the abbot of Montecassino, Desiderius of Benevento, who mediated between the prince and the Emperor Henry IV on the latter's descent into Italy (1081).

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: Jordan forsook his erstwhile papal ally in exchange for an imperial investiture.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: Though Robert Guiscard and his brother Roger marched against him, Roger was recalled to Sicily and the expedition fell apart.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: In 1085, on Robert's death, Jordan supported Bohemond, the elder son, over Roger Borsa, the eldest by Sichelgaita, who was his own sister-in-law, he having married Gaitelgrima, another daughter of Prince Guaimar IV of Salerno.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: For the next three years, Bohemond held Apulia with the assistance of well-trained Capuan armies.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: In that same year, the pope died and the antipope Clement III continued to claim the papacy.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: In hopes of curbing the influence of Clement and united his interests with those of the papacy once again, he pressured the College of Cardinals to elect Desiderius of Montecassino as successor Gregory.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: At the same time, Roger Borsa freed the captured imperial prefect of Rome in opposition to the pretensions of Jordan and the Papal Curia, which had refused confirmation of Roger's archiepiscopal candidate for Salerno.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: The move backfired and Desiderius, under pressure from Jordan to accept, was elected pope as Victor III.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: With the aid of armies from Jordan and the Countess Matilda of Tuscany, Victor took the Vatican Hill from Clement on 1 July 1086.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: The pope remained lukewarm to his new job until Jordan suggested that only through decisive action could the good fortune of his beloved abbey of Montecassino be sustained.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: This led to an important synod at Benevento (1087), where Clement was excommunicated, lay investiture outlawed, and war with the Saracens of Africa declared.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: The remainder of Jordan's career was not notable and he died in November 1090 or 1091 in Piperna (near Terracina) and was buried in the monastery he had long supported, Montecassino, leaving a young son named Richard who succeeded him.

evidence.title: Jordan I of Capua
evidence.text: His other sons, Robert and Jordan, would also succeed to the Capuan throne some day, and he left one unnamed daughter.

claims.description: Find the paternal grandfather of Jordan II of Capua

quotes.text: Jordan I  (after 1046 – 1091), count of Aversa and prince of Capua from 1078 to his death, was the eldest son and successor of Prince Richard I of Capua and Fressenda, a daughter of Tancred of Hauteville and his second wife, also named Fressenda, and the nephew of Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily.
